architectural_implications.after: A ~15-line orchestration prompt plus multiple on-demand skills pulled into context only when needed.
architectural_implications.before: A single multi-hundred-line prompt containing all policies, procedures and tool usage guidance.
architectural_implications.consequence: Lower baseline context occupancy and higher task accuracy (71% to 92%), but correctness now depends on the model correctly deciding when to load a skill.
architectural_implications.observation: Instructions that were permanently resident in the system prompt move to lazily-retrieved skill documents.

architectural_implications.after: Python/Bash executed against raw files, returning only a reduced result such as top-N JSON.
architectural_implications.before: Bespoke data-dump tool that inlines raw data (e.g., CSV) into the context window.
architectural_implications.consequence: ~28x token reduction per task (216k to 7.6k) and less tool-schema maintenance, at the cost of depending on code-generation reliability and an execution sandbox.
architectural_implications.observation: Pre-processing of data into context is replaced by code the agent writes and executes.

architectural_implications.after: Isolated sessions with full observability and metrics matching the orchestrator.
architectural_implications.before: Hardcoded subagents tightly coupled to the orchestrator with formatting mismatches.
architectural_implications.consequence: Parallelizable, independently measurable sub-tasks, but requires an explicit interface contract to avoid boundary formatting failures.
architectural_implications.observation: Monolithic delegation logic is replaced by subagents invoked as callable agents.

article_ideas.angle: Diagnose regressions as architecture defects by looking for policy collisions and missing dedicated tools rather than rewording instructions.
article_ideas.audience: Applied AI engineers maintaining long-lived production agents
article_ideas.based_on: Conflicting policies in different parts of a monolithic system prompt led to model confusion.
article_ideas.thesis: Prompt growth does not degrade an agent by making it vaguer; it degrades it by co-locating mutually contradictory instructions in one context, so the failure signature is a specific wrong answer (a hallucinated promotion multiplier instead of the supplied 3.1x) and the correct response is structural, not more clarifying prose.

article_ideas.angle: Reframe tool design around data reduction at the execution layer rather than pre-processing everything into context.
article_ideas.based_on: Replacing custom data-dump tools with Python scripts dropped token usage from 216k to 7.6k per task.
article_ideas.thesis: A small set of general primitives (code execution, filesystem access) subsumes many narrow tools because the model's generated code becomes the dispatch mechanism and only the reduced result enters the context window; the token savings are a symptom of a deeper shift from schema design to code-generation trust.
article_ideas.title: The 28x Rule: Stop Building a Tool Catalog and Start Shipping Primitives

article_ideas.angle: Treat skill loading as a retrieval problem requiring precision/miss metrics, not a prompt-formatting trick.
article_ideas.based_on: Skills provide packaged, composable information that Claude pulls into context only when needed.
article_ideas.thesis: Skills convert a loud failure (context bloat and conflicting residency) into a quiet one (missed or wrong skill selection), so adopting progressive disclosure without selection-level evals is trading a diagnosable problem for an invisible one.

article_ideas.thesis: Choosing between tool, skill and subagent is a coupling decision as much as a capability decision, because the pre-refactor system's formatting failures came from the orchestrator-to-subagent seam rather than from any single component, so interfaces must be explicit and testable before decomposition pays off.

evidence_quotes.text: Swapping a 416-line legacy prompt for a 15-line prompt with 5 on-demand skills increased eval success from 71% to 92%.

core_insights.generalization: Any agent whose instructions have grown by appending one procedure per feature can likely be decomposed into a thin orchestration prompt plus lazily-loaded capability documents, with accuracy and cost both improving.
core_insights.insight: Replacing a monolithic system prompt with a short orchestration prompt plus on-demand 'skills' (progressive disclosure) converts a large token-cost/attention penalty into a measurable accuracy gain: a 416-line prompt swapped for a 15-line prompt + 5 skills moved eval success from 71% to 92%, indicating the win comes from loading domain procedures only when the task requires them rather than from the prompt content itself.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a concrete, measurable refactor pattern: treat domain procedures, guidelines and templates as retrievable modules rather than permanent system-prompt real estate, which simultaneously reduces context bloat and raises task success.

evidence_quotes.text: Replacing custom data-dump tools with Python scripts dropped token usage from 216k to 7.6k per task.
Trust the model's ability to write and execute code to inspect data rather than pre-processing everything into context.

core_insights.generalization: Prefer a small set of general primitives over a large catalog of narrow tools; the model's ability to write code becomes the dispatch mechanism, and the context window only receives the computed answer.
core_insights.insight: Foundational computer-like primitives (code execution via Bash/Python, filesystem access) can replace many bespoke single-purpose tools, collapsing context consumption by roughly 28x — token usage fell from 216k to 7.6k per task when a raw data-dump tool was replaced with a Python script returning top-N JSON.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes tool design: instead of encoding every analysis as a rigid tool schema plus pre-processed data in context, let the model write code against raw data and return only the reduced result, which directly attacks token cost, latency and pre-processing maintenance.

evidence_quotes.text: Callable agents in CMA allow subagents to run in isolated sessions with full observability and metrics matching the orchestrator.

core_insights.generalization: Any multi-agent topology should be judged partly on whether per-delegate telemetry is comparable to the parent's, otherwise failure attribution and cost accounting break down at the boundary.
core_insights.insight: Subagents implemented as callable agents run in isolated sessions yet emit observability metrics that match the orchestrator's, meaning delegation does not create an observability gap — a prerequisite for treating subagents as an organizational boundary rather than a debugging hazard.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Observability parity between orchestrator and delegated agents determines whether a multi-agent decomposition is operable in production; if subagent telemetry is a second-class citizen, isolation becomes a liability.

core_insights.generalization: When an agent regresses on previously-passing tasks, look for mutually inconsistent instructions co-resident in context and for reasoning tasks that lack a dedicated tool, rather than adding clarifying prose.
core_insights.insight: The failure signature of an overgrown prompt is not degraded tone but specific wrong answers: conflicting policy statements inside one prompt led to model confusion, and the agent hallucinated a promotion multiplier instead of using the supplied 3.1x value, while without a dedicated tool it took a winding path through raw CSV data during the daily low-stock sweep.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It ties a structural defect (policy collision and missing tool support in one monolithic context) to reproducible eval failures, which lets engineers diagnose architecture rather than rewording instructions.

evidence_quotes.text: Communication breakdowns between orchestrators and hardcoded subagents caused formatting failures.

core_insights.generalization: Every delegation boundary needs an explicit, testable interface contract (schema, formatting, error semantics); otherwise decomposition trades context bloat for integration failures.
core_insights.insight: Orchestrator-to-subagent interfaces are themselves a failure surface: communication breakdowns between orchestrators and hardcoded subagents caused formatting failures, implying the decomposition decision must account for the contract between caller and callee, not just capability placement.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It warns that splitting work into subagents can introduce new failure modes at the boundary, so the tool/skill/subagent choice is a coupling decision as much as a capability decision.

core_insights.generalization: Decomposition frameworks should be indexed by the kind of content being extracted and the runtime property required, not by feature count.
core_insights.insight: The practical decision procedure implied by the case study is a routing rule over three primitives: short prompt for orchestration and core behavior, skills for on-demand domain knowledge and procedures, foundational tools (bash, file reading) for capability, and callable subagents for isolated parallelizable sub-tasks with observability — applied when the prompt exceeds manageable length or shows regression and excessive token cost.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It converts the 'tool, skill or subagent?' question from intuition into an allocation rule based on what the artifact is (behavior, knowledge, capability, parallel work) and what property is needed (token economy, isolation, parallelism, observability).

core_insights.why_it_matters: It makes architecture changes falsifiable: regression tasks catch breakage while LLM-judge tasks probe qualitatively-shaped failure modes, and the loop discipline prevents prompt edits from being judged by vibes.

source.title: Tool, skill, or subagent? Decomposing an agent that outgrew its prompt

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: William Steuk
  • Channel: Claude
  • Main topic: Decomposing and refactoring complex AI system prompts into modular tools, skills, and subagents
  • Purpose: To educate engineers and developers on how to refactor and optimize complex, prompt-heavy AI agents into clean, modular architectures using tools, skills, and subagents. William Steuk from Anthropic discusses the architectural evolution of AI agents that have outgrown their system prompts. Using an inventory management agent called 'StockPilot' as a case study, he explores how bolting on too many capabilities leads to regressions, degraded performance, and context bloat. He presents a systematic approach to refactoring — breaking down monolithic prompts into composable primitives: tools, skills, and subagents (specifically callable agents in Claude Managed Agents), and using evals ('hill climbing') to measure performance improvements.

Topic Map

Introduction and Problem Statement

  • Explanation: Introduction of William Steuk and the common anti-pattern of agent prompts growing to hundreds of lines due to continuous capability additions.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents that start out successful often degrade in performance as business requirements and capabilities are continually bolted onto the system prompt.
    • Monolithic system prompts lead to regressions in areas the agent was previously accelerating in.
  • Examples:
    • A system prompt growing to several hundred lines with dozens of tools and subagents.
  • Terminology:
    • Applied AI
    • system prompt
    • regression
    • StockPilot
  • Why it matters: Context bloat and architectural complexity cause AI agents to fail at specific tasks due to conflicting instructions and lack of modularity.

Introducing StockPilot and Evals

  • Explanation: Walkthrough of StockPilot, an inventory management agent for an outdoor-gear retailer, and its evaluation framework consisting of 12 eval tasks across 5 grader types.
  • Key claims:
    • StockPilot manages 250 SKUs, 3 warehouses, 12 suppliers, and 90 days of sales history.
    • Evals are divided into deterministic regression tasks (R-tasks) and non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge failure mode tasks (F-tasks).
  • Examples:
    • R1 (stock lookup), R8 (promo-month forecast), F1 (daily low-stock sweep).
  • Terminology:
    • evals
    • graders
    • deterministic
    • non-deterministic
    • LLM-as-a-judge
  • Why it matters: Without robust evaluations, engineers cannot quantitatively measure whether architectural changes improve or degrade agent performance.

Anatomy of the Architectural Failure

  • Explanation: Detailed root cause analysis of why StockPilot failed specific evals (dropping from 83% to 62% success rate), including context window pollution, conflicting policy instructions, and missing tool support.
  • Key claims:
    • Model took an inefficient path because reasoning tasks were performed without proper dedicated tools.
    • Communication breakdowns between orchestrators and hardcoded subagents caused formatting failures.
    • Conflicting policies in different parts of a monolithic system prompt led to model confusion.
  • Examples:
    • R8 promo-month forecast hallucinating a promotion multiplier instead of using 3.1x.
    • F1 daily low-stock sweep taking a winding path through raw CSV data.
  • Terminology:
    • context pollution
    • orchestrator
    • subagent
    • root cause analysis
  • Why it matters: Understanding exact points of failure allows engineers to apply the correct architectural primitive rather than adding more text to the system prompt.

Refactoring Architecture: Tools, Skills, and Subagents

  • Explanation: Step-by-step refactoring using Claude Managed Agents (CMA), swapping legacy prompts for short prompts, loading organizational procedures on demand via skills, and implementing callable subagents.
  • Key claims:
    • Skills provide packaged, composable information that Claude pulls into context only when needed.
    • Code execution (Bash/Python) replaces rigid tool definitions for data analysis and file traversal.
    • Callable agents in CMA allow subagents to run in isolated sessions with full observability and metrics matching the orchestrator.
  • Examples:
    • Replacing 416-line system prompt with a 15-line prompt and 5 on-demand skills.
    • Replacing raw CSV dumping tool with a Python script that returns top-N JSON.
  • Terminology:
    • skills
    • progressive disclosure
    • code execution
    • Claude Managed Agents
    • callable agents
  • Why it matters: Modular architectures drastically reduce token consumption, execution latency, and cost while improving eval success rates.

Key Points

The Danger of Monolithic System Prompts

  • Explanation: Appending new business requirements and tool instructions directly into a system prompt leads to context bloat, token inefficiency, and model confusion.
  • Evidence: StockPilot system prompt grew to 400+ lines, causing eval performance to drop from 83% to 62%.
  • Practical implication: Keep system prompts short and focused only on core orchestration and foundational instructions.

Progressive Disclosure via Skills

  • Explanation: Instead of stuffing all procedures into the system prompt, package domain knowledge into modular 'skills' that the agent loads on demand.
  • Evidence: Swapping a 416-line legacy prompt for a 15-line prompt with 5 on-demand skills increased eval success from 71% to 92%.
  • Practical implication: Use skills for reference material, guidelines, and templates that are only needed for specific tasks.

Lean on Computer-Like Primitives

  • Explanation: Grant agents foundational tools like code execution (Bash/Python) and file system access rather than building rigid, custom single-purpose tools for every action.
  • Evidence: Replacing custom data-dump tools with Python scripts dropped token usage from 216k to 7.6k per task.
  • Practical implication: Trust the model's ability to write and execute code to inspect data rather than pre-processing everything into context.

Hill-Climbing with Evals

  • Explanation: Optimize agent architecture iteratively by running automated test suites, triaging failures, updating agent design, and measuring improvements.
  • Evidence: Running 'uv run evals --agent before' followed by architectural iterations and re-running evals.
  • Practical implication: Treat agent development like software engineering: measure performance regressions and improvements programmatically.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Agent Decomposition Framework

  • How it works: Deconstructs an bloated agent prompt into foundational primitives by separating orchestration, specialized knowledge, and parallel execution.
  • Components:
    • Short System Prompt (orchestration and core behavior)
    • Skills (on-demand domain knowledge and procedures)
    • Tools (foundational capabilities like bash and file reading)
    • Callable Subagents (isolated, parallelizable sub-tasks with observability)
  • When to use: When an AI agent's prompt exceeds manageable lengths and exhibits regression in performance or excessive token costs.

Examples & Case Studies

StockPilot failed R8 promo-month forecast because the model hallucinated a promotion multiplier instead of using 3.1x due to conflicting policies in a 400-line prompt.

  • Illustrates: Context pollution and policy contradiction in monolithic prompts.
  • Lesson: Separate policies and forecasting instructions into targeted skills or subagents.

StockPilot's daily low-stock sweep (F1) failed because it dumped 395 rows of CSV data into context, causing context-over-context misses.

  • Illustrates: Inefficient data transfer between tools and the model.
  • Lesson: Replace rigid data-dump tools with code execution where the model writes Python scripts to query data in the sandbox.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Audit existing agent system prompts for length and bloat.
    • Extract static policies and procedures into modular skill files.
    • Implement automated evaluations to establish an empirical baseline.
  • Strategic:
    • Adopt progressive disclosure so agents only load context when required.
    • Favor code execution and file system primitives over hyper-specific custom tools.
    • Use managed agent platforms (like CMA) to offload orchestration harness, infrastructure, memory, and scaling concerns.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • When should a capability be implemented as a skill versus a callable subagent?
    • How do non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge graders correlate with production reliability?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Replacing rigid custom tools with Python code execution drops token usage significantly while maintaining task success. (technical benchmark)
  • Claude Managed Agents (CMA) provides native primitives for callable subagents with persistent threads and isolated sandboxes. (product architecture)

Notable Quotes

"Tool, skill, or subagent? Decomposing an agent that outgrew its prompt" (at 0:13) "Every choice was defensible when made. Bottlenecks in capability emerge from accumulation." (at 5:34) "Simple composable agents scale with model intelligence" (at 72:05)

  • Monolithic agent system prompts cause capability accumulation, context bloat, and regression.

## Overview
- **Speaker**: William Steuk
- **Channel**: Claude
- **Main topic**: Decomposing and refactoring complex AI system prompts into modular tools, skills, and subagents
- **Purpose**: To educate engineers and developers on how to refactor and optimize complex, prompt-heavy AI agents into clean, modular architectures using tools, skills, and subagents.
William Steuk from Anthropic discusses the architectural evolution of AI agents that have outgrown their system prompts. Using an inventory management agent called 'StockPilot' as a case study, he explores how bolting on too many capabilities leads to regressions, degraded performance, and context bloat. He presents a systematic approach to refactoring — breaking down monolithic prompts into composable primitives: tools, skills, and subagents (specifically callable agents in Claude Managed Agents), and using evals ('hill climbing') to measure performance improvements.
## Topic Map
### Introduction and Problem Statement
- **Explanation**: Introduction of William Steuk and the common anti-pattern of agent prompts growing to hundreds of lines due to continuous capability additions.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents that start out successful often degrade in performance as business requirements and capabilities are continually bolted onto the system prompt.
  - Monolithic system prompts lead to regressions in areas the agent was previously accelerating in.
- **Examples**:
  - A system prompt growing to several hundred lines with dozens of tools and subagents.
- **Terminology**:
  - Applied AI
  - system prompt
  - regression
  - StockPilot
- **Why it matters**: Context bloat and architectural complexity cause AI agents to fail at specific tasks due to conflicting instructions and lack of modularity.
### Introducing StockPilot and Evals
- **Explanation**: Walkthrough of StockPilot, an inventory management agent for an outdoor-gear retailer, and its evaluation framework consisting of 12 eval tasks across 5 grader types.
- **Key claims**:
  - StockPilot manages 250 SKUs, 3 warehouses, 12 suppliers, and 90 days of sales history.
  - Evals are divided into deterministic regression tasks (R-tasks) and non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge failure mode tasks (F-tasks).
- **Examples**:
  - R1 (stock lookup), R8 (promo-month forecast), F1 (daily low-stock sweep).
- **Terminology**:
  - evals
  - graders
  - deterministic
  - non-deterministic
  - LLM-as-a-judge
- **Why it matters**: Without robust evaluations, engineers cannot quantitatively measure whether architectural changes improve or degrade agent performance.
### Anatomy of the Architectural Failure
- **Explanation**: Detailed root cause analysis of why StockPilot failed specific evals (dropping from 83% to 62% success rate), including context window pollution, conflicting policy instructions, and missing tool support.
- **Key claims**:
  - Model took an inefficient path because reasoning tasks were performed without proper dedicated tools.
  - Communication breakdowns between orchestrators and hardcoded subagents caused formatting failures.
  - Conflicting policies in different parts of a monolithic system prompt led to model confusion.
- **Examples**:
  - R8 promo-month forecast hallucinating a promotion multiplier instead of using 3.1x.
  - F1 daily low-stock sweep taking a winding path through raw CSV data.
- **Terminology**:
  - context pollution
  - orchestrator
  - subagent
  - root cause analysis
- **Why it matters**: Understanding exact points of failure allows engineers to apply the correct architectural primitive rather than adding more text to the system prompt.
### Refactoring Architecture: Tools, Skills, and Subagents
- **Explanation**: Step-by-step refactoring using Claude Managed Agents (CMA), swapping legacy prompts for short prompts, loading organizational procedures on demand via skills, and implementing callable subagents.
- **Key claims**:
  - Skills provide packaged, composable information that Claude pulls into context only when needed.
  - Code execution (Bash/Python) replaces rigid tool definitions for data analysis and file traversal.
  - Callable agents in CMA allow subagents to run in isolated sessions with full observability and metrics matching the orchestrator.
- **Examples**:
  - Replacing 416-line system prompt with a 15-line prompt and 5 on-demand skills.
  - Replacing raw CSV dumping tool with a Python script that returns top-N JSON.
- **Terminology**:
  - skills
  - progressive disclosure
  - code execution
  - Claude Managed Agents
  - callable agents
- **Why it matters**: Modular architectures drastically reduce token consumption, execution latency, and cost while improving eval success rates.
## Key Points
### The Danger of Monolithic System Prompts
- **Explanation**: Appending new business requirements and tool instructions directly into a system prompt leads to context bloat, token inefficiency, and model confusion.
- **Evidence**: StockPilot system prompt grew to 400+ lines, causing eval performance to drop from 83% to 62%.
- **Practical implication**: Keep system prompts short and focused only on core orchestration and foundational instructions.
### Progressive Disclosure via Skills
- **Explanation**: Instead of stuffing all procedures into the system prompt, package domain knowledge into modular 'skills' that the agent loads on demand.
- **Evidence**: Swapping a 416-line legacy prompt for a 15-line prompt with 5 on-demand skills increased eval success from 71% to 92%.
- **Practical implication**: Use skills for reference material, guidelines, and templates that are only needed for specific tasks.
### Lean on Computer-Like Primitives
- **Explanation**: Grant agents foundational tools like code execution (Bash/Python) and file system access rather than building rigid, custom single-purpose tools for every action.
- **Evidence**: Replacing custom data-dump tools with Python scripts dropped token usage from 216k to 7.6k per task.
- **Practical implication**: Trust the model's ability to write and execute code to inspect data rather than pre-processing everything into context.
### Hill-Climbing with Evals
- **Explanation**: Optimize agent architecture iteratively by running automated test suites, triaging failures, updating agent design, and measuring improvements.
- **Evidence**: Running 'uv run evals --agent before' followed by architectural iterations and re-running evals.
- **Practical implication**: Treat agent development like software engineering: measure performance regressions and improvements programmatically.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Agent Decomposition Framework
- **How it works**: Deconstructs an bloated agent prompt into foundational primitives by separating orchestration, specialized knowledge, and parallel execution.
- **Components**:
  - Short System Prompt (orchestration and core behavior)
  - Skills (on-demand domain knowledge and procedures)
  - Tools (foundational capabilities like bash and file reading)
  - Callable Subagents (isolated, parallelizable sub-tasks with observability)
- **When to use**: When an AI agent's prompt exceeds manageable lengths and exhibits regression in performance or excessive token costs.
## Examples & Case Studies
### StockPilot failed R8 promo-month forecast because the model hallucinated a promotion multiplier instead of using 3.1x due to conflicting policies in a 400-line prompt.
- **Illustrates**: Context pollution and policy contradiction in monolithic prompts.
- **Lesson**: Separate policies and forecasting instructions into targeted skills or subagents.
### StockPilot's daily low-stock sweep (F1) failed because it dumped 395 rows of CSV data into context, causing context-over-context misses.
- **Illustrates**: Inefficient data transfer between tools and the model.
- **Lesson**: Replace rigid data-dump tools with code execution where the model writes Python scripts to query data in the sandbox.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Audit existing agent system prompts for length and bloat.
  - Extract static policies and procedures into modular skill files.
  - Implement automated evaluations to establish an empirical baseline.
- **Strategic**:
  - Adopt progressive disclosure so agents only load context when required.
  - Favor code execution and file system primitives over hyper-specific custom tools.
  - Use managed agent platforms (like CMA) to offload orchestration harness, infrastructure, memory, and scaling concerns.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - When should a capability be implemented as a skill versus a callable subagent?
  - How do non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge graders correlate with production reliability?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Replacing rigid custom tools with Python code execution drops token usage significantly while maintaining task success. (technical benchmark)
- Claude Managed Agents (CMA) provides native primitives for callable subagents with persistent threads and isolated sandboxes. (product architecture)
## Notable Quotes
> "Tool, skill, or subagent? Decomposing an agent that outgrew its prompt" (at 0:13)
> "Every choice was defensible when made. Bottlenecks in capability emerge from accumulation." (at 5:34)
> "Simple composable agents scale with model intelligence" (at 72:05)
## Compressed Summary
- Monolithic agent system prompts cause capability accumulation, context bloat, and regression.
- Refactoring involves shortening system prompts and loading organizational procedures on-demand via skills.
- Use foundational computer primitives like Python execution instead of rigid custom tools to reduce token usage.
- Callable subagents allow parallel exploration and clean context isolation for complex sub-tasks.
- Iterative 'hill-climbing' using automated evals validates architectural improvements.
- **Keywords**: agents, prompts, skills, tools, evals, refactoring
- **Core insight**: Decomposing bloated agent prompts into composable tools, on-demand skills, and isolated subagents drastically reduces token costs and improves reliability.
